paragraphs: Mixed-integer linear programming represents optimization problems using variables and linear constraints, with some variables required to take integer values. Learning methods often represent these problems as graphs linking variables to constraints. Graph neural networks then build representations by exchanging information along those links, but their local processing can limit the relationships they capture.

This paper proposes a neural backbone that treats variables and constraints as two types of elements. Its dual attention mechanism performs two operations in parallel: self-attention connects elements of the same type, while cross-attention connects variables with constraints. This gives the representation a way to combine relationships within each group with relationships between the groups.

The authors evaluate the backbone on three representative tasks spanning whole problem instances, individual elements, and solver states. They report consistent improvements over conventional graph neural network architectures. These findings support attention as a useful foundation across several learning tasks associated with optimization; they concern the quality of learned modeling, rather than a general guarantee of solving these hard optimization problems efficiently.
icml-2026-a-general-neural-backbone-for-.tldr: A dual-attention backbone models relationships within and between MILP variables and constraints, outperforming conventional graph neural networks on three representative tasks.

paragraphs: Mendelian randomization uses genetic variants as instruments to estimate causal effects from observational data. Its usefulness depends on assumptions about how those variants relate to other influences on the outcome. In particular, genetic instruments should be independent of unobserved confounders. Environmental correlations arising through population structure or assortative mating can violate that requirement and compromise causal inference.

The paper uses data from multiple environments or populations to address this problem. Rather than treating the observed genetic instruments as automatically valid, it learns representations intended to recover hidden exogenous components within them. The central idea is that variation across environments can help uncover components suitable for causal analysis despite confounding in the original instruments.

The authors provide theoretical insights into the circumstances under which the learned components can function as valid instruments. They also report evidence from simulations and semi-synthetic experiments using All of Us Biobank genetic data. The contribution therefore combines a proposed recovery method with conditional theoretical support and experimental validation, rather than establishing that representation learning always repairs invalid instruments.
icml-2026-addressing-instrument-outcome-.tldr: A representation-learning framework uses multiple environments to recover genetic instrument components that can support causal inference under theoretically studied conditions.

paragraphs: AlphaGRPO aims to help a unified multimodal model use its existing understanding more effectively during generation. It applies Group Relative Policy Optimization to models combining autoregressive and diffusion components. The targeted capabilities include inferring implicit user intentions when generating images and diagnosing and correcting mismatches in outputs through self-reflective refinement.

A central component is DVReward, which turns a complex request into smaller questions that can be checked individually. An LLM produces questions about semantic requirements and output quality, and a multimodal LLM evaluates them. This decomposition gives the reinforcement-learning process more interpretable feedback than a single holistic judgment and is intended to provide stable supervision for complex generation requests.

The authors report robust improvements on GenEval, TIIF-Bench, DPG-Bench, and WISE. They also report significant improvements on GEdit despite not training on editing tasks. These results suggest that the approach can transfer some gains beyond its training tasks. The stated contribution is to activate and coordinate capabilities already present in the model, without relying on external knowledge injection.
icml-2026-alphagrpo-unlocking-self-refle.tldr: AlphaGRPO uses decomposed, verifiable feedback to improve multimodal generation and self-correction, with reported editing gains even without editing-task training.

paragraphs: Network alignment asks which vertex in one graph corresponds to which vertex in another. Connections provide clues, but node features can also carry useful evidence. This paper studies recovery when both weighted edges and node features are observed, so the matching procedure can draw on two sources of information about the same hidden correspondence.

The authors introduce a featured correlated Gaussian Wigner model. In this mathematical setting, an unknown permutation connects the vertices of two correlated graphs, and the node features are correlated according to that same permutation. They characterize optimal information-theoretic thresholds for recovering either the entire correspondence or only part of it. These thresholds describe the recovery limits within the proposed model.

The paper also introduces QPAlign, an efficient algorithm based on a quadratic programming relaxation. Experiments show strong performance on synthetic and real datasets, while theoretical results provide guarantees for the procedure and its convergence. Together, the contributions address both how much information recovery requires and how an efficient method can exploit the available graph and feature evidence.
icml-2026-attributed-network-alignment-s.tldr: The paper characterizes recovery limits for graph alignment with node features and introduces QPAlign, an efficient algorithm with theoretical and empirical support.

paragraphs: AudioMosaic learns representations for general audio understanding from unlabeled recordings. Much earlier work trains audio encoders through reconstruction objectives. This paper instead develops contrastive learning, an approach whose use in audio has been constrained partly by the cost of creating suitable paired inputs and supporting the large batches used during pretraining.

The method constructs paired inputs by masking spectrogram patches along time and frequency dimensions. These masked views provide the training pairs through a computationally efficient augmentation procedure. The encoder learns discriminative representations at the utterance level, with the goal of capturing information that remains useful when the dataset, application domain, or acoustic conditions change.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on multiple standard benchmarks and strong transfer across datasets, domains, and acoustic settings. They also find that integrating the pretrained encoder with large language models improves audio perception. The findings connect a relatively simple way of constructing training views to useful general-purpose audio representations, including representations that can support a larger language-based system.
icml-2026-audiomosaic-contrastive-masked.tldr: AudioMosaic uses efficient time–frequency masking for contrastive audio pretraining, producing transferable representations and improving audio perception in LLM integrations.

paragraphs: CG-MLLM brings 3D captioning and high-resolution 3D generation into one multimodal language-model framework. The paper targets a gap in existing approaches: their outputs often consist of low-resolution meshes or coarse structural representations, which do not directly capture fine geometric detail. The challenge is to accommodate spatial content alongside the tokens handled by language-based models.

The architecture separates these modeling responsibilities through a Mixture-of-Transformer design. A TokenAR transformer handles token-level content, while a BlockAR transformer handles content organized into blocks. A pretrained vision-language backbone is connected with a specialized 3D variational autoencoder latent space, allowing standard tokens and spatial blocks to interact over long contexts within the integrated model.

The authors report that CG-MLLM significantly outperforms existing multimodal language models at generating high-fidelity 3D objects. The architectural significance is the combination of shared interaction and specialized processing: language and spatial representations can communicate, while different transformer components handle their respective forms of content. This supports both describing 3D content and generating detailed objects within the same framework.
icml-2026-cg-mllm-captioning-and-generat.tldr: CG-MLLM combines token-level and block-level transformers to support 3D captioning and high-resolution generation in one multimodal model.

paragraphs: Introducing AI into a workplace creates two linked decisions: whether to delegate a task and how carefully to check the result. This paper models a rational worker choosing both actions according to their own costs and benefits. It then evaluates the chosen workflow using an institutional objective, which can differ from the worker’s private objective.

The analysis shows that optimal behavior can change sharply with verification ability. In these phase transitions, arbitrarily small differences in a worker’s ability to verify outputs can produce substantially different delegation and oversight choices. This means that similar workers need not respond similarly to the same AI capability when their incentives and verification reliability interact.

Under the model, AI can improve institutional worker quality for strong verifiers while reducing it for others who rationally delegate too much and check too little. That decline can occur even when baseline task success improves and workers have no behavioral biases. The result identifies an incentive-based mechanism for widening quality disparities, rather than attributing the problem solely to irrational trust in AI.
icml-2026-delegation-and-verification-un.tldr: A formal model shows how rational delegation and verification choices can make AI amplify institutional quality differences between workers.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering combines different representations of the same samples to discover groups. Anchor-based approaches reduce the cost of spectral clustering by linking samples to representative anchors. The paper argues that existing methods weaken information exchange by handling the shared graph and final discrete cluster assignments as largely separate optimization problems.

DRMC first uses sample–anchor associations to construct similarity representations at the sample level, rather than directly combining views only in anchor space. This step is designed to strengthen similarity within clusters and separation between clusters. A discrete feedback module then learns the spectral embedding and cluster assignments together, aligning the continuous embedding with the discrete assignment matrix through an orthogonal transformation.

The resulting partition is fed back into construction of the shared graph, so assignments can refine the structure that helped produce them. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show significant advantages over existing state-of-the-art approaches. The central contribution is this feedback between continuous representations and discrete group membership, allowing clustering decisions to participate in graph refinement instead of appearing only at the end.
icml-2026-discretely-refined-multi-view-.tldr: DRMC improves multi-view clustering by feeding discrete cluster assignments back into the shared similarity graph through aligned embedding learning.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a model use examples in its input to perform a task. This paper investigates how transformers acquire that ability across modalities using small models trained on synthetic classification problems. The controlled setting lets the authors manipulate both data statistics and architecture while examining the internal mechanisms that emerge.

The study first revisits learning within a single modality. Several earlier findings replicate, but rotary position embeddings can delay the emergence of in-context learning circuits. Moving to multiple modalities reveals an asymmetry: after pretraining on highly diverse data from a primary modality, relatively low complexity in a secondary modality is sufficient for multimodal in-context learning to appear in the studied setting.

Mechanistic analysis identifies an induction-style process that copies labels from matching examples in the context. Multimodal training refines and extends this mechanism across modalities. These results connect observed learning behavior to specific circuit dynamics and provide a controlled experimental setting for further study. Their scope is the small synthetic-task transformers examined, rather than a direct demonstration across all multimodal language models.
icml-2026-dissecting-multimodal-in-conte.tldr: Controlled transformer experiments reveal asymmetric data requirements for multimodal in-context learning and trace it to circuits that copy labels from matching examples.

paragraphs: Long reasoning chains can help models solve difficult problems, but they can also contain substantial redundant computation. The paper examines the observation that longer reasoning is often unrelated to correctness and can sometimes reduce accuracy. Its central empirical finding is that reasoning models can possess an implicit sense of when to stop, even when ordinary sampling fails to expose it.

The authors introduce SAGE, a sampling approach intended to reveal this existing capacity for efficient reasoning. The intervention focuses on how reasoning is sampled, connecting the model’s latent stopping capability to the process that produces an actual reasoning trajectory. This matters because a capability inside the model is useful only if inference can reliably access it.

They then incorporate SAGE into group-based reinforcement learning through mixed sampling, producing SAGE-RL. The aim is to learn efficient patterns discovered through SAGE so they carry over to standard single-attempt inference. Across multiple challenging mathematical benchmarks, the authors report marked improvements in both accuracy and efficiency, supporting the use of sampling discoveries as training signals for more economical reasoning.
icml-2026-does-your-reasoning-model-impl.tldr: SAGE exposes empirically observed stopping capabilities in reasoning models, and SAGE-RL trains those efficient patterns into standard single-attempt inference.

paragraphs: Rare spikes in gradient size can destabilize neural-network training by causing oversized updates and disturbing the optimizer’s accumulated state. Gradient clipping helps, but its threshold needs tuning and it truncates large gradients without distinguishing their statistical context. GradientStabilizer addresses the magnitude of these training signals using information accumulated over time.

The method preserves the current gradient’s direction while replacing its magnitude with a stabilized estimate computed from running gradient-norm statistics. The authors prove that this stabilized magnitude stays uniformly bounded on spike steps, independently of how large the spike is. They also show how that bound controls the evolution of internal state in adaptive optimizers.

Experiments span FP16 language-model pretraining, FP4 quantization-aware pretraining, ImageNet classification, reinforcement learning, and time-series forecasting. The authors report consistently improved stability, wider ranges of stable learning rates, and less divergence than clipping-based alternatives. They also report substantially reduced sensitivity of Adam to weight-decay strength. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support magnitude stabilization as a lightweight intervention across the tested training settings.
icml-2026-gradientstabilizer-fix-the-nor.tldr: GradientStabilizer preserves gradient direction while statistically stabilizing magnitude, with bounded responses to spikes and improved stability across tested training settings.

paragraphs: Training a smaller reasoning model on outputs from a stronger teacher does not always improve its reasoning. This paper identifies a substantial mismatch between the teacher’s style and the student’s existing output distribution as a major factor in such failures. Stronger answers can therefore be ineffective fine-tuning material when their presentation diverges from the student’s learned patterns.

TESSY generates training sequences through cooperation between teacher and student. The models alternate in producing style and non-style tokens, aiming to retain the teacher’s reasoning capabilities while keeping the resulting sequences stylistically consistent with the student. This makes compatibility with the learner an explicit part of data synthesis.

In code-generation experiments, GPT-OSS-120B serves as teacher and Qwen3-8B as student. Fine-tuning on teacher-generated data produces reported performance drops of 3.25% on LiveCodeBench-Pro and 10.02% on OJBench. TESSY instead produces improvements of 11.25% and 6.68%, respectively. These findings support the importance of student-consistent synthetic data in the tested setting and show that teacher strength alone does not determine fine-tuning success.
icml-2026-how-to-fine-tune-a-reasoning-m.tldr: TESSY interleaves teacher and student generation to create stylistically compatible fine-tuning data, reversing reported performance declines in code-generation experiments.

paragraphs: Relational deep learning turns database tables and their relationships into a graph for neural prediction. Existing approaches commonly keep that graph fixed to preserve relational meaning under a full-resolution design principle. This paper asks whether the structure can instead be learned while retaining that semantic consistency.

FROG makes the roles of tables learnable, allowing them to contribute as nodes and edges during message passing. Its role-driven mechanisms determine how information moves through those relationships, enabling graph structure and neural representations to be optimized together. This reframes graph construction as part of learning rather than a fixed choice made before training.

To preserve semantics, FROG adds constraints based on functional dependencies, regularizing representations across table and entity levels. These constraints connect structural flexibility with the relationships the database is supposed to encode. Extensive experiments report improvements over existing approaches and examine how table roles affect downstream tasks. The findings support learning how tables participate in prediction while explicitly maintaining consistency with relational structure, rather than assuming a fixed graph is always the best representation.
icml-2026-is-fixing-schema-graphs-necess.tldr: FROG jointly learns database graph structure and neural representations through adaptable table roles constrained to preserve relational semantics.

paragraphs: Many combinatorial problems can be expressed as quadratic objectives over binary variables, with penalties encoding constraints. Relaxing the variables to values between zero and one makes gradient-based optimization possible. However, a local minimum of the resulting continuous problem can contain fractional values or violate the original constraints, leaving the solver with an unusable answer.

The paper establishes sufficient structural conditions on quadratic penalties that prevent these failures. When those conditions hold, every local minimizer of the relaxed problem is binary and feasible. This is a guarantee about the validity of local solutions; it does not say that every such solution is globally optimal.

The authors examine existing formulations where available, explain failures, and construct alternatives meeting their conditions. Examples include open-pit mining, knapsack, and traveling salesman formulations. They show how these constructions support the use of projected gradient descent and Adam to obtain valid binary solutions. The contribution identifies when continuous optimization has a trustworthy connection to the original discrete problem, rather than relying on the hope that relaxed solutions will become valid.
icml-2026-local-minima-in-quadratic-pena.tldr: The paper gives sufficient penalty conditions ensuring that every local minimum of certain relaxed binary optimization problems is binary and feasible.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can train reasoning models using feedback on final answers, despite the many intermediate steps needed to reach them. This paper develops a theory of how that learning progresses in transformers performing compositional reasoning tasks. It asks how outcome-only rewards can support improvement over extended reasoning sequences.

The theory shows that training on mixed difficulties can create an implicit curriculum without an explicit ordering of examples. Easier problems become learnable first and help make harder problems accessible. When difficulty changes smoothly across the training distribution, persistent gradients on easier tasks support progress on slightly harder ones, producing what the authors call a relay regime.

When the difficulty spectrum instead contains abrupt gaps, the theory predicts long plateaus followed by grokking-like transitions. Thus, the progression depends on how training problems bridge levels of difficulty, not merely on including easy and hard examples. The analysis adapts Fourier methods on finite groups, and synthetic experiments validate the predicted mechanisms. The results provide a theoretical account of curriculum emergence within the studied reasoning setting.
icml-2026-on-the-emergence-of-implicit-c.tldr: A theory of RLVR explains how mixed-difficulty training creates an implicit curriculum, with smooth difficulty spectra supporting steady progress and gaps producing plateaus.

paragraphs: Checking an open-ended mathematical solution requires detecting flaws in its reasoning. This paper identifies error detection as the main bottleneck in automatic verification and proposes a workflow organized around finding any reason to reject a candidate. Multiple verifiers operate in parallel, and a flaw identified by any one of them causes rejection.

The progressive version combines this pessimistic decision rule with fine-grained decomposition of proofs. Breaking the argument into smaller components makes verification more focused. The authors report that this approach improves both verification accuracy and token efficiency compared with extended chains of thought and mainstream verification workflows.

Their analysis also finds annotation errors in existing benchmarks that cause those benchmarks to underestimate the method’s effectiveness with stronger models. To test verification within a broader solving process, they apply it to IMO 2025 and MathArena Apex 2025 problems using state-of-the-art models. They report substantial gains in efficiency and accuracy. The contribution connects targeted error detection with practical improvements in solving difficult mathematical problems, while highlighting how benchmark labels can distort evaluation.
icml-2026-pessimistic-verification-for-o.tldr: Parallel flaw detection and fine-grained proof decomposition improve reported mathematical verification accuracy and token efficiency.

paragraphs: In reinforcement learning from human feedback, a policy learns to produce outputs that receive high scores from a reward model. That process can go wrong when the policy exploits accidental scoring patterns instead of better matching human intent. The paper focuses on how this problem grows as the policy’s output distribution changes during training.

R2M introduces a lightweight reward-modeling framework that uses the policy’s evolving hidden states as feedback. Rather than depending solely on semantic representations from a pretrained language model, the reward model also receives information reflecting the policy’s current internal behavior. The aim is to keep reward evaluation aligned with the policy as reinforcement learning changes it.

The approach treats reward modeling as a continuing interaction with the learner, connecting the scoring mechanism to the distribution it currently evaluates. This directly addresses the authors’ diagnosis that semantic information alone does not efficiently track policy shifts. The stated contribution is a promising direction for improving reward models through real-time policy feedback, without claiming that this mechanism completely eliminates reward exploitation.
icml-2026-real-time-aligned-reward-model.tldr: R2M uses a policy’s evolving hidden states to help its reward model track distribution shifts during reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models distribute specialized components across devices and route each token to a selected subset. Their efficiency depends partly on how that work is distributed. This paper investigates a vulnerability arising when inference lacks explicit load-balancing constraints: unusual inputs can concentrate routing on the same experts and leave other devices underused.

The authors demonstrate that out-of-distribution prompts can send all tokens to the same top-k expert set. This creates a hardware bottleneck even though the architecture is designed for efficient scaling. RepetitionCurse is their black-box, model-agnostic strategy for exposing the issue through repetitive token patterns, linking input structure to harmful routing concentration.

On widely deployed mixture-of-experts models running on eight-GPU clusters, the method increases time to first token by 20% to 148%. That delay affects how long users wait before a response begins and can violate service-level expectations. The results identify inference-time routing balance as an operational security concern: selective computation can become a denial-of-service weakness when adversarial inputs repeatedly concentrate the selected work.
icml-2026-repetitioncurse-measuring-and-.tldr: RepetitionCurse demonstrates how repetitive inputs concentrate MoE routing, increasing time to first token by 20%–148% in tested eight-GPU deployments.

paragraphs: Distillation accelerates text-to-image generation by teaching a student to replace a longer generation process with fewer steps. Matching image quality does not necessarily preserve how the generator responds to changes in its starting noise. The paper identifies loss of that sensitivity as a problem for control methods that optimize or manipulate the initial noise.

The authors trace the issue to objectives that match teacher and student outputs at individual input points. Such matching can flatten the student’s input–output landscape and suppress the teacher’s local geometric behavior. Geometry-Aware Distillation adds alignment of Jacobian-vector products with respect to input noise, teaching the student how the teacher’s output changes along small input perturbations.

Experiments across multiple text-to-image paradigms and noise-driven control tasks show substantial recovery of sensitivity and improved diversity while retaining high visual fidelity. The result emphasizes a functional property of the generator that ordinary output matching can miss. Preserving nearby responses matters when a downstream method needs to steer generation through the noise input, rather than merely obtain a visually convincing sample.
icml-2026-restoring-initial-noise-sensit.tldr: Geometry-Aware Distillation matches responses to noise perturbations to restore controllability and improve diversity in accelerated text-to-image models.

paragraphs: Soft objects change shape under both environmental forces and robot actions, making their behavior difficult to simulate over extended interactions. SoMA addresses real-to-simulation modeling of these coupled effects. The paper identifies limitations in approaches based on predefined physics or learned dynamics that do not explicitly incorporate robot-conditioned control.

SoMA represents the scene using learned 3D Gaussian splats and combines deformable dynamics, environmental forces, and robot joint actions in a shared latent neural space. This unified representation lets the simulator model interactions while remaining conditioned on the robot’s actions. The approach learns these dynamics without relying on predefined physical models.

The authors report a 20% improvement in resimulation accuracy and generalization for real-world robot manipulation, together with stable simulation of complex tasks such as long-horizon cloth folding. They also report generalization beyond observed trajectories. These findings matter because reproducing a recorded motion and responding coherently to actions beyond that recording are different demands. SoMA’s contribution is to address both through an action-conditioned learned simulator for deformable objects.
icml-2026-soma-a-real-to-sim-neural-simu.tldr: SoMA jointly models soft-body dynamics, environmental forces, and robot actions, reporting improved resimulation and generalization with stable long-horizon manipulation.

paragraphs: Graph edit distance measures the smallest number of edits needed to transform one graph into another. Computing it is NP-hard. Some scalable hybrid methods predict a node-matching matrix and extract several candidate mappings, but candidates from the same deterministic matrix can be highly correlated, limiting the range of edit paths explored.

DiffGED treats node matching as a generative task. A diffusion model produces several diverse matching matrices simultaneously, from which candidate mappings can be extracted efficiently. This changes where diversity enters the process: the method generates different matching hypotheses instead of repeatedly extracting alternatives from one fixed prediction.

The authors report that the resulting diversity helps avoid suboptimal solutions and yields solution quality close to exact computation. On real-world datasets, DiffGED produces diverse edit paths with accuracy comparable to exact solutions while running faster than existing hybrid approaches. These are empirical results rather than a guarantee of exact recovery on every graph pair. The contribution is a way to broaden candidate exploration while reducing the inefficiency of repeated extraction.
icml-2026-towards-generative-graph-match.tldr: DiffGED generates diverse graph-matching hypotheses with diffusion, achieving near-exact empirical edit-distance quality faster than existing hybrid approaches.

paragraphs: An LLM service can control cost by choosing among models or by adjusting the computation spent within a chosen model. These decisions are often handled separately. Model selection offers only the available discrete model sizes, while additional computation on a fixed model can encounter diminishing returns and limits imposed by that model’s capacity.

Unified Inference Scaling places model selection and inference-time computation in one optimization space. UniScale implements this idea as an online contextual multi-armed bandit using LinUCB. It learns how to choose inference configurations in context, while efficiency-aware learning and cost modeling support optimization over a large action space.

Evaluations report a consistently better and more fine-grained quality–cost trade-off across diverse, changing inference scenarios. The significance is that model capacity and extra computation can be considered together when allocating resources. A decision about spending more computation therefore need not be isolated from the decision about which model receives it. The findings support joint adaptive allocation in the tested deployment scenarios rather than a single fixed configuration for all requests.
icml-2026-uniscale-adaptive-unified-infe.tldr: UniScale jointly learns model selection and inference-time compute allocation online, improving reported quality–cost trade-offs in dynamic scenarios.

paragraphs: Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures predict latent representations rather than reconstructing observations such as pixels. Standard versions are deterministic, limiting their ability to express uncertainty for planning and control. VJEPA extends this approach to learn distributions over future latent states through a variational objective operating in latent space.

The authors connect this formulation with predictive state representations and Bayesian filtering. They show that its latent variables can provide sufficient information for control when those variables preserve task-relevant predictive information. A second variant, BJEPA, combines a learned dynamics expert with modular prior experts through a Product of Experts, supporting constraint-aware predictions and swapping priors without additional training.

Experiments cover Noisy-TV systems, nonlinear and image-based benchmarks, STL-10 with a vision transformer encoder, and DMC Cheetah-run. The results show greater robustness to high-variance nuisance distractions than reconstruction-based world-model baselines. Together, these findings support probabilistic latent prediction as a route to uncertainty-aware world models, while the control interpretation remains conditional on retaining the predictive information relevant to the task.
icml-2026-vjepa-variational-joint-embedd.tldr: VJEPA adds probabilistic latent prediction to JEPA, while BJEPA incorporates modular priors; experiments show improved robustness to nuisance distractions.

paragraphs: A diffusion model uses timestep embeddings to tell its denoising network where it is in the generation process and which noise level it should handle. This paper investigates whether that conditioning space can carry additional information. The question matters for both malicious information injection and reliable provenance, beyond the usual focus on image quality and generation speed.

Shadow Timestep Embedding explores this temporal space as a side channel. The authors find that different timesteps have different representational capabilities and can encode auxiliary information. They also show that information encoded there can be used for attack and defense purposes through the scheduler interface, connecting the temporal signal to how generation is controlled.

The theoretical analysis treats timestep embeddings as position-encoding mappings and derives a mutual-coherence evaluation to explain the separability of disjoint timestep intervals. This provides an account of why distinct temporal regions can support distinguishable representations. The contribution is to identify and analyze an information-bearing channel inside diffusion conditioning, showing that the timestep signal has implications for security and provenance as well as denoising.
icml-2026-watch-your-step-information-in.tldr: Shadow Timestep Embedding reveals diffusion timestep conditioning as a side channel for auxiliary information with attack and defense applications.

paragraphs: Merging language models can combine capabilities without retraining, but mixture-of-experts models introduce a routing problem. Their router decides which experts process each token. The paper identifies routing breakdown: merging perturbs router parameters so that tokens are sent to unsuitable experts, undermining the specialized capabilities the merged model is meant to retain.

The authors trace this sensitivity to the router’s nonlinear softmax and discrete top-k selection, with pretraining load-balancing constraints further amplifying the effect. Because fine-tuned experts specialize differently, even modest routing errors can seriously damage performance. HARC addresses the problem using second-order curvature information to recalibrate the merged router without training.

The calibration has a closed-form solution that can be computed efficiently using matrix-free conjugate gradients. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that HARC mitigates routing breakdown across diverse merging baselines and substantially improves performance. The findings show why combining expert parameters is only part of successful MoE merging: the router must also remain aligned with the capabilities of the experts it selects.
icml-2026-when-model-merging-breaks-rout.tldr: HARC uses training-free curvature-aware calibration to repair disrupted MoE routing after model merging and improve reasoning and code-generation performance.
